# Introduction

If you have ever brought home a pot of supermarket basil and watched it collapse within a fortnight, this book is for you. I have done it more times than I like to admit. For years I thought I was simply bad with plants. I was wrong. Most of the time it was the window, the pot or the watering can, and all three are things you can change.

I started growing herbs in 2020, in a rented flat in Sheffield with a north-facing kitchen and an east-facing bedroom. I wanted fresh basil for pasta, and I did not want to pay for a new pot every other week. Six years and two rented flats later, I have a row of herbs that keep going for months, and a fair idea of why the early ones did not.

This is a short, practical book for people who grow on windowsills because that is all they have. You might rent, so you cannot drill holes or put up shelves. Your windows might face the wrong way. You might have a radiator under every sill, net curtains you are not allowed to take down, and a landlord who frowns at drips on the paintwork. That was me. Everything in here has been tried on ordinary UK windows, through ordinary grey winters.

## How the book works

There are five chapters, and each one builds on the last.

- Chapter 1 shows you how to read the light at each of your windows, so you know where a herb will grow before you buy it.
- Chapter 2 covers pots, compost and drainage that fit a narrow sill and keep your landlord happy.
- Chapter 3 goes through seven herbs that cope indoors, with what each one needs.
- Chapter 4 is about watering, which is where most indoor herbs come to grief.
- Chapter 5 shows you how to harvest so your plants keep growing, and what to do when the mint takes over.

Read chapter 1 before you buy anything. It costs nothing, and it will save you more money than the rest of the book put together. After that, dip in as you need to.

## What this book is not

It is not a botany textbook, and I am not a professional grower. I am someone who has killed a lot of basil and learnt from it. I tell you what has worked for me, on my windows, and I say so when I am not sure. Plants vary, homes vary and the weather certainly varies, so treat my advice as a starting point and watch what your own plants tell you.

Right. Let's go and look at your windows.

# Chapter 1: Read your windows before you buy a plant

Your basil did not die because you are bad with plants. It died because of where you put it.

My first basil plant lived on the kitchen sill. It seemed the obvious place: next to the chopping board, handy for cooking, with the window right there. That window faces north. Within three weeks the plant was tall, pale and floppy, with long bare stems between small leaves. It leaned so hard towards the glass that it looked as if it was trying to escape. I watered it, fed it and, I admit, talked to it. Nothing helped.

In the end I moved it to the bedroom, which has an east-facing window. Within a couple of weeks the new growth was shorter, greener and bushier. Same plant, same compost, same me. The only thing that had changed was the light.

That was the moment I stopped buying herbs first and looking at windows second.

## Why light matters more than anything else

Plants make their food from light. Indoors, even a window that looks bright to you gives a plant much less light than it would get outside. The walls, the frame and the ceiling block most of the sky. Your eyes adjust to a dim room without you noticing. A plant cannot.

When a herb does not get enough light, it stretches towards whatever light there is. Gardeners call this going leggy. The stems grow long and weak, the leaves get smaller and paler, and the plant flops. If you see this, the answer is almost never more water or more feed. It is more light.

## Which way does each window face?

Start by finding out which way each of your windows faces. Use the compass on your phone: stand with your back to the room, face the glass, and read the direction you are looking.

Here is the rough rule for UK homes, and it matches what I have seen on my own windows.

- South-facing windows get the most sun, for most of the day. They are the best spot for herbs that like it hot and bright, such as rosemary and thyme.
- East-facing windows get the morning sun and then go into shade. Mine is my most reliable spot for basil.
- West-facing windows get the afternoon and evening sun. They can be as good as east, and warmer in summer.
- North-facing windows get little or no direct sun. They are bright enough for a few tough herbs, but not for basil.

Most windows face somewhere in between, such as south-east. Treat those as a mix of the two.

## Count the hours, not just the direction

The direction is only half the story. What matters to the plant is how many hours of direct sun actually reach the sill. A south-facing window with a tall building across the road might get less sun than an east-facing one with an open view.

So watch your windows. On a sunny day, check each sill every hour or so and note when the sun starts to fall on it and when it leaves. You do not need to be exact. "Sun from about eight until eleven" is plenty.

In my current flat, the front room faces east, and in summer the sun reaches the sill from early morning until late morning. The kitchen faces north and gets none at all. That tells me straight away where the basil goes and where it does not.

## Winter is a different window

In a UK winter, the sun sits much lower in the sky and the days are short. A window that gets a few hours of sun in June might get very little in December, especially if there are buildings or trees opposite. Herbs grow slowly in winter whatever you do, and that is normal.

Do your light check twice if you can: once in summer and once in winter. If you are starting in winter, expect slow growth, and do not panic when your plants seem to sit still for a couple of months. Mine pick up again every spring as the days get longer.

## Things that steal light

Once you know your windows, look at what sits between the sky and your sill.

- Net curtains. If yours hang close to the glass, behind the plants, they cut light your herbs would otherwise get. If you can, hang them on the room side of the sill, so the herbs sit between the net and the glass.
- Dirty glass. A wipe of the inside, and the outside where you can safely reach it, makes a difference you can see.
- Blinds left half down. Open them fully during the day.
- Other plants. A big leafy plant on the same sill shades the small ones behind it.

## A one-week light diary

Here is the one job for this chapter. For one week, keep a light diary: one line per window, each day. Write the direction, roughly when direct sun reaches the sill and when it leaves. Add anything that gets in the way, such as nets or a building opposite.

My first diary, in the first flat, looked like this:

- Kitchen, north: no direct sun. Bright but flat light all day.
- Bedroom, east: sun on the sill from about half past seven to half past ten.
- Bathroom, north, frosted glass: no direct sun. Dim.

By the end of the week you will know which window is your best, which is your second best, and which ones to give up on for herbs. That is worth more than any plant label.

## If you only have a north window

Do not give up. Mint, parsley and chives have all grown for me on a bright north sill. They were slower and less bushy than in the east window, but good enough to cut. Basil, rosemary and thyme have not managed it. Chapter 3 goes through each herb in turn.

If your only window is dim, you could look into a small grow light. I have not used one myself, so I cannot tell you which kind to buy, but they are worth reading about if your windows let you down.

***

Your basil probably died because of its window, not because of you. Spend a week watching your windows before you buy another plant, and you will know where it should go.

# Chapter 2: Pots, compost and drainage for a narrow sill

The pot your herb came in was made to get it from a greenhouse to a shop shelf. It was never meant to be its home.

I learnt that slowly. In my first flat I bought a lovely glazed pot for my basil, white with a blue rim, and planted the basil straight into it. The pot had no hole in the bottom. Every time I watered, the water had nowhere to go. After a few weeks the compost smelled sour, the lower leaves went yellow and the whole plant wilted, even though the compost was soaking. When I tipped it out, the roots at the bottom were brown and slimy. I had drowned it in a pot that looked great in photos.

My second mistake was a long trough with mint at one end and parsley at the other. Right, so the trick with mint is to give it its own pot. I learnt that the hard way. It ate the parsley.

This chapter is about getting the basics under your herbs right: the pot, the compost and somewhere for the water to go.

## Every pot needs a hole

If you take one thing from this chapter, take this. Every pot a herb grows in needs at least one drainage hole in the bottom. Without one, water collects at the bottom of the pot, the roots sit in it, and they rot.

You can still use pretty pots with no holes. Use them as an outer pot. Plant the herb in a plain plastic pot with holes, stand that inside the pretty one, and tip out any water that collects in the outer pot after you water. The plant gets drainage and you get the look you wanted.

## Measure your sill first

UK windowsills are often narrow, and rented ones can be very narrow. My kitchen sill is only about fifteen centimetres deep. Before you buy pots, measure the depth and length of each sill you plan to use, and write it in your light diary from chapter 1.

A pot that hangs over the edge is a pot waiting to be knocked off. For most herbs on a narrow sill, a pot a little bigger than the one the plant came in is plenty. Bigger is not always better indoors: a large pot holds a lot of wet compost that a small plant cannot use, and it stays wet for longer.

## Terracotta or plastic?

Both work. They behave differently, and you can use that.

- Terracotta (unglazed clay) lets water evaporate through its sides, so the compost dries out faster. It is heavier, which makes it steadier on a sill. It suits rosemary and thyme, which like to dry out between drinks.
- Plastic holds water for longer and is light. It suits mint and parsley, which like their compost to stay moist.

Most of my herbs live in plastic pots inside nicer outer pots. My rosemary and thyme are in terracotta.

## Saucers and trays

If you rent, your landlord will not thank you for water rings on the paintwork. Put a saucer or a tray under every pot. A long plastic tray that fits your sill works well for a row of small pots, and it catches the drips when you water.

The catch is that a saucer full of water undoes the good work of the drainage hole. After you water, wait half an hour or so, then tip away anything left in the saucer.

## Compost

Use a bagged peat-free multi-purpose compost from a garden centre or DIY shop. Do not dig soil from a park or a friend's garden. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot, drains badly and can bring pests indoors.

Rosemary and thyme like a grittier, faster-draining mix. When I pot these, I mix in a few handfuls of horticultural grit or perlite, both sold in bags near the compost. For basil, mint, parsley and chives, plain multi-purpose compost has been fine for me. Read the bag for anything it says about feeding.

## Splitting a supermarket pot

Here is something I wish someone had told me in my first year. A supermarket pot of basil is usually not one plant. It is lots of seedlings crammed together in a small pot, all fighting for the same water and light. The last one I bought had more stems than I could be bothered to count.

When I get a new pot home, I split it. I water it first, tip the whole thing out and gently pull the root ball apart into three or four clumps. Each clump goes into its own pot with fresh compost, and I water them in. They sulk for a few days, then they grow far better than the crowded pot ever did. I have done the same with parsley, as long as I am gentle with the roots.

## A few sill safety points

- Keep pots on the inside sill. A pot on an outside ledge above a street or a path can fall and hurt someone.
- Check the window still opens and shuts without knocking anything over.
- If there is a radiator under the sill, expect the compost to dry out faster in winter. Chapter 4 covers what to do about it.
- On cold winter nights, leaves pressed against the glass can be damaged by the cold. Leave a small gap between the plants and the window.

***

Your one job for this chapter: measure your sills, then write a shopping list. For each window, note how many pots will fit, what size, and whether you want terracotta or plastic. Add a bag of peat-free compost, a small bag of grit and enough saucers. Then you are ready to choose your herbs.

# Chapter 3: Seven herbs that cope indoors

Not every herb wants to live on a windowsill. These seven have lived on mine, some happily and some under protest.

When I started, I bought whatever the supermarket had and lined it all up on the kitchen sill. The mint carried on as if nothing had happened. The parsley and chives slowed down but kept going. The basil gave up first, then the coriander, and a little thyme plant just sat there for months, neither growing nor dying, until I moved it. That first year taught me that each herb has its own idea of a good window, and the trick is to match them.

For each herb below you get the light it needs, how it likes to be watered and what has happened on my sills. Chapter 4 goes into watering in more detail.

## Choosing a healthy plant

Whether you buy from a supermarket or a garden centre, take a minute to look the plant over before it goes in your basket. I look for:

- Leaves that are green all the way down, with no yellow ones at the bottom.
- Firm stems that stand up on their own.
- No small flies around the compost, and nothing sticky or speckled under the leaves.
- Compost that is damp, not dry and shrunk away from the side of the pot.

If roots are poking out of the bottom of the pot, the plant has been in it a while. That is fine, but repot it soon after you get it home.

## Basil

**Light:** your sunniest window. An east or south sill. Not north, in my experience.

**Water:** when the top of the compost feels dry. I water in the morning, so it is not sitting cold and wet overnight.

**Warmth:** basil hates the cold. Keep it away from draughts and from cold glass on winter nights.

**On my sills:** basil is the herb that taught me the most. Split the supermarket pot (chapter 2), give it your best window and pinch out the tops (chapter 5). In winter mine slows almost to a stop, and I accept that. Some years I let it go at the end of the summer and start again with a fresh pot in spring.

## Mint

**Light:** copes with less light than most herbs. It has grown on my north kitchen sill.

**Water:** likes compost that stays moist. Do not let it dry out completely.

**Pot:** always its own. Its roots spread sideways and fill a pot fast.

**On my sills:** the easiest herb I grow, and the bossiest. When the roots fill the pot, usually after a year, I tip it out, cut the root ball into pieces and pot one piece back up. The rest go to friends.

## Parsley

**Light:** a bright sill, east or west. It has managed on my north sill, more slowly.

**Water:** keep the compost evenly moist.

**On my sills:** both flat-leaf and curly have grown for me; I prefer flat-leaf for cooking. Parsley is slow from seed, so I buy a pot and split it. Cut the outer stalks first. In my experience a parsley plant gives its best leaves in its first year. In its second year it tends to flower, and the leaves get fewer and tougher, so that is when I start a new one.

## Chives

**Light:** tolerant. A bright north sill will do, an east one is better.

**Water:** moderate. Let the top of the compost dry a little between drinks.

**On my sills:** the toughest herb on this list. Cut whole leaves a few centimetres above the compost and they grow back. If mine flowers, I enjoy the purple heads for a week, then cut the flowering stems off at the base, because they are tough to eat.

## Thyme

**Light:** as much sun as you can give it. A south sill if you have one, or your best east sill.

**Water:** sparingly. Let the compost dry out between waterings. Terracotta and a gritty mix help (chapter 2).

**On my sills:** thyme is a slow, woody little plant indoors, and it has never been as bushy for me as the thyme I have seen in friends' gardens. The quickest way to kill it is to water it as often as the mint. Leave it alone more than feels right.

## Rosemary

**Light:** the sunniest sill you have.

**Water:** let it dry out between drinks, and never leave it sitting in water.

**Size:** rosemary is a shrub. A young plant is happy on a sill for a while, but it will want a bigger pot in time.

**On my sills:** I kept one rosemary for three years in the east window. It grew slowly but steadily. I lost a second one in its first winter, and I am fairly sure I killed it by watering it as often as I did in summer.

## Coriander

**Light:** a bright sill, east or west.

**Water:** keep the compost moist.

**Watch out for:** coriander likes to run to seed. It sends up a flower stem, and the leaves turn thin and feathery. Drying out and heat seem to make it happen sooner.

**On my sills:** the least reliable herb on this list. I treat it as short-lived: I sow a few seeds in a pot every few weeks in spring and summer, and cut the leaves while they are young.

## Herbs I would leave until later

Over the years I have also tried dill, sage and oregano indoors. Sage and oregano did reasonably well in the east window, much like thyme: slow, woody and happiest when I left them alone. Dill grew tall and floppy and fell over. None of them earned a permanent place on my sills, but if you have a sunny south window you may have more luck. Start with the seven in this chapter, and experiment once those are growing well.

## The seven at a glance

| Herb | Best window | Water | Pot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basil | East or south | When the top is dry | Plastic, split from a supermarket pot |
| Mint | Any bright sill, even north | Keep moist | Its own pot, always |
| Parsley | East or west, copes with north | Keep moist | Plastic |
| Chives | East, copes with north | Let the top dry a little | Plastic or terracotta |
| Thyme | South or your best east | Let it dry out | Terracotta, gritty mix |
| Rosemary | Your sunniest sill | Let it dry out | Terracotta, gritty mix |
| Coriander | East or west | Keep moist | Plastic, sow little and often |

***

Pick two or three herbs that match your best window from chapter 1, and start with those. Once they are growing well, add one more at a time.

# Chapter 4: Watering without drowning them

Most indoor herbs die from too much water, not too little.

I did not believe that for a long time. In my first flat I watered every herb every morning, the way you might feed a cat. It felt kind. The mint loved it. The basil went yellow at the bottom. The rosemary lasted until its first winter, then gave up, and when I tipped it out the compost was wet right through. I had been watering on a timetable instead of watering the plant.

## Check before you water

The fix is simple: check the compost every time, and only water when the plant needs it.

The finger test is the one I use most. Push a finger into the compost, up to the first knuckle. If it feels dry at your fingertip, water. If it feels damp, leave it and check again tomorrow.

The lift test is useful for small pots. Pick the pot up just after you water it, and notice how heavy it feels. Pick it up again a few days later. A dry pot feels much lighter, and after a week or two you can tell by weight alone.

## How to water

When a plant does need water, give it a proper drink. Pour water slowly onto the compost, not the leaves, until it starts to run out of the hole in the bottom. Then wait half an hour or so and tip away whatever is left in the saucer. A good soak followed by a chance to dry out is better than a little splash every day.

I use tap water that has stood in a jug until it reaches room temperature, so it is not cold on the roots.

For basil, I often water from the bottom instead. I stand the pot in a bowl with a few centimetres of water for ten minutes or so. When the top of the compost looks darker, I lift it out and let it drain on the draining board. This keeps the leaves dry and gets water to the bottom of the pot, where the roots are.

## Different herbs, different thirsts

Chapter 3 gives a watering line for each herb. Roughly, they fall into three groups:

- Keep moist: mint, parsley and coriander. Check them often, and do not let them dry out completely.
- In between: basil and chives. Water when the top of the compost is dry.
- Let them dry out: thyme and rosemary. Water only when the compost is dry well below the surface, and less often than feels right.

## A small watering kit

You do not need much, but a few things make watering on a narrow sill easier and kinder to the paintwork.

- A small watering can or jug with a narrow spout, so the water goes on the compost and not over the sill.
- A bowl big enough to stand one pot in, for watering from the bottom.
- An old tea towel kept near the window, for drips.

## Summer, winter and the radiator

In summer, when the sun is strong and the plants are growing fast, you may need to water some herbs every day or two. In winter, growth slows right down and most herbs need far less. My rosemary goes a week or more between drinks in winter.

The radiator makes this tricky. In many UK homes there is a radiator under the window, and when the heating is on it can dry out a small pot quickly. Check those pots more often in winter. But do not go back to a timetable, and never stand a pot directly on a hot radiator.

The combination that has killed most of my herbs is a cold window, a dark winter day and compost that never dries. If your herbs are on a cold sill in winter, water less, not more.

## Reading the signs

Your plants tell you when the watering is wrong, if you know what to look for.

Too much water:

- Lower leaves turning yellow.
- The plant wilting even though the compost is wet.
- A sour smell from the compost.
- Small flies hovering over the compost. In my experience they come with compost that stays wet.

If you see these, stop watering until the top of the compost is dry, empty every saucer and check the drainage hole is not blocked.

Too little water:

- The plant wilting, with dry compost.
- Leaf edges turning crisp and brown.
- The pot feeling very light when you lift it.

If you see these, give the plant a good drink, ideally from the bottom, and check it more often from now on.

## A word on feeding

Herbs in small pots use up the food in their compost after a while. In spring and summer I give basil, mint and parsley a general liquid feed, at the strength on the label, every couple of weeks. Thyme and rosemary get much less. I do not feed anything in winter, when the plants are barely growing.

## Going away

For a weekend, water everything well the day before you leave and move the pots out of the hottest sun. For longer, ask a neighbour or a friend. Show them the finger test before you go, or they will kill your rosemary with kindness, exactly as I did.

***

For the next week, check every pot each morning with your finger before you water. Note in your diary which ones actually needed a drink. By the end of the week you will know each plant's thirst better than any timetable could.

# Chapter 5: Harvest so it keeps growing

The best thing you can do for a basil plant is eat it, as long as you pick it the right way.

My first basil plants never got bushy. I picked the biggest leaves, one at a time, from the bottom of the stems, because that seemed the polite thing to do. After a month each plant was a tall bare stick with a tuft of leaves on top. Then a friend showed me how to pinch out the top of a stem, just above a pair of leaves. A week later, two new shoots were growing where there had been one. I have picked basil that way ever since.

## When to start picking

A new plant needs time to settle. After I split a supermarket pot or repot a herb, I leave it alone for two or three weeks, until I can see fresh growth at the tips. Then I start picking, a little at a time. I pick in the morning when I can, because the leaves seem firmer then, and I always use clean scissors or my fingernails rather than tearing the stems.

## The rule of a third

My rule of thumb for every herb is never to take more than about a third of a plant at one time. The plant needs its leaves to keep growing. If you strip it bare, it has nothing left to grow back with, especially indoors where light is short. Small, regular harvests are better than one big one.

## Basil

Pinch or snip the top of each stem just above a pair of leaves. Two new shoots grow from that point, and the plant gets bushier. Do not pull off the big bottom leaves: they are feeding the plant.

When you see small flower buds at the tips, pinch them out. Once basil flowers, mine has always put less effort into leaves.

## Mint

Cut whole stems, low down, just above a pair of leaves. Mint grows back quickly, so you can be more generous with it than with anything else on your sill. If it starts to look straggly, cut the whole plant back hard, and in my experience it comes back fresher.

## Parsley

Cut the outer stalks near the base, where they come out of the compost. New stalks grow from the centre, so always leave the middle alone.

## Chives

Cut a handful of whole leaves a few centimetres above the compost. Do not trim the tops off all the leaves like a haircut, because the cut ends go brown and it looks sad.

## Thyme and rosemary

Snip the soft green tips. Never cut back into the old, bare, woody part of the stem, because in my experience it does not grow back from there. Little and often suits both of them.

## Coriander

Cut the outer leaves while they are young. When it starts to send up a flower stem, harvest what you can and sow a new pot.

## Drying rosemary and thyme

Woody herbs dry well. Tie a few stems together with string and hang them somewhere warm, dry and out of direct sun, away from the steam of the kettle. When the leaves crumble between your fingers, strip them into a clean, dry jar with a lid and label it. Soft herbs such as basil and parsley I freeze rather than dry, because dried they lose most of their taste for me.

## What to do with all the mint

At some point your mint will produce more than you can use. This is the happiest problem in this book. Here is what I do with mine:

- Make fresh mint tea: a few stems in a mug of hot water.
- Chop it into salads, yoghurt or new potatoes.
- Make a simple mint sauce with chopped mint, vinegar and a little sugar.
- Freeze it. Chop the leaves, pack them into an ice cube tray, top up with water and freeze. The cubes go straight into a pan or a glass.
- Give it away. Stems of mint stood in a glass of water have grown roots for me within a couple of weeks. Potted up, they make a good present for a friend with a sill of their own.

## A typical week on my sills

In midsummer, a normal week looks something like this. Early in the week I pinch the tops out of the basil for a tomato salad. Midweek I cut a few stems of mint for tea and a small handful of chives for scrambled eggs. At the weekend I take some outer stalks of parsley for whatever I am cooking, and snip a few rosemary tips for roast potatoes. Nothing gets more than a light trim, and by the following weekend every plant has filled the gaps. In winter the same sills give me much less, and I buy the rest without feeling guilty about it.

## Keeping cut herbs fresh

Rinse herbs before you eat them. If you cut more than you need, basil keeps best for me in a glass of water on the kitchen counter, like cut flowers. In my fridge it goes black within a day or two. Parsley, coriander and mint last a few days in the fridge, wrapped in damp kitchen paper inside a box or a bag.

***

This week, pinch out the top of every basil stem, and cut one stem of mint for a cup of tea or the freezer. Then watch what happens over the next fortnight.

# Conclusion: your next steps

When I killed my first basil plant, I thought the problem was me. It was not. It was a north window, a pot with no hole and a watering timetable. None of those things needed talent to fix. They needed someone to point them out.

Here is everything in this book in five lines:

- Read your windows first, and put each herb where its light is.
- Use pots with holes, peat-free compost and a saucer you empty.
- Choose herbs that match your best window, and start with two or three.
- Check before you water, and water less in winter.
- Harvest a little and often, from the top, and never more than a third.

If you do one thing this week, keep the light diary from chapter 1. If you do two, split a supermarket pot of basil and put the clumps on your best sill. In a month you will have more basil than you can eat, and you will know why.

After that, add one herb at a time. Give each new one the window it wants, watch it for a few weeks and adjust. Your sills will not look like mine, and they should not. The fun is in finding out what your own windows can do.

# About the author

::: demo
A demo book made with the AI Book Writing and Amazon KDP Toolkit. Sam Rowe is a fictional author.
:::

I am Sam Rowe. I have grown herbs on the windowsills of two rented flats in Sheffield since 2020, and killed more basil than I like to admit along the way. By day I work in a library. In the evenings I can usually be found turning pots round so they grow straight, or taking photos of them for Instagram.

I wrote this book because the advice I found when I started assumed a garden, a greenhouse or at least a sunny window. I had none of those. Everything in here comes from my own windows, my own mistakes and the plants that put up with me.

If this book helped you, an honest review on the store where you bought it helps other readers decide whether it is right for them. Thank you for reading.
